Your average was 641.9 kVAR. That reactive tail is riding every single production shift — and your transformer is hauling it right alongside your real load of 1,348.7 kilowatts. The financial consequence is direct. The field is generating approximately $27,729 in energy waste per monthly dataset. Annualized, that's roughly $337,375 in direct reactive losses. **REND1 — Voltage Health | April 2026**

The voltage field on REND1 is elevated above nominal on average — the monthly average is 477.2 volts against the 480-volt nominal reference — but the more important story is what happens during production loading events.

Twelve distinct triangular voltage dip events are labeled and visible in the V-view across the full thirty-day period. These are not clustered in one production week — they are distributed across the entire month, which tells you this is a chronic recurring condition, not an isolated anomaly. The dip readings cluster tightly in the 455 to 461 volt range. The deepest labeled dip is 455.3 volts, which represents a depression of approximately 24.7 volts below the 480-volt nominal — that is a 5.2 percent sub-nominal condition.

Other labeled dips: 456.7 V, 460.6 V, 458.1 V, 456.5 V, 457.4 V, 456.4 V, 457.2 V, 457.0 V, 456.2 V, 459.4 V, and a second instance at 456.5 V. Every single one of these is below nominal.

The minimum recorded voltage of 9.5 volts is the floor captured during scheduled shutdown intervals — not a sustained operational reading — so that figure is not a supply quality concern on its own. The high of 492.8 volts during low-load periods is within acceptable range.

What matters for device health is the production-period pattern: motors and compressors running in the 455 to 461 volt range during load peaks are drawing higher current than they should. In a food processing and cold storage environment, where compressor motors and VFDs run continuously during production, that elevated current draw compounds with the harmonic distortion already present in the field — measured at 5.8 percent iTHD. The combined effect is accelerated insulation aging, elevated contact wear on motor starters and contactors, and increased thermal stress on winding insulation.

Device health risk for REND1 voltage conditions: **moderate to high.** The dips are not catastrophic individually, but their chronic, distributed repetition across a full month of production is the concern. Equipment stress accumulates invisibly until it doesn't.

REND1.operational_stress_interpretation:
**REND1 — Operational Stress | April 2026**

The REND1 transformer is operating under sustained, compounding stress. The facility is running a clear weekly production cycle — electrically active for approximately 70 to 75 percent of the month, with scheduled shutdown valleys appearing roughly every five to six days. During those active production periods, the transformer is loaded at or above the 1,390 kVA supply target for the majority of operational hours.

That is a high sustained loading condition. When you layer in a power factor averaging 83.4 percent, you are asking the transformer to carry significantly more apparent power than the real work it is doing justifies. The gap between 1,348.7 kilowatts of real demand and 1,390 kVA of apparent supply represents the reactive overhead that is riding along with every production shift, heating conductors, stressing insulation, and occupying transformer capacity that could otherwise serve additional productive load.

The 1,701.1 amp peak current reading is the sharpest single indicator of stress on this bus. Conductor and transformer winding heating scales with the square of current — I-squared-R heating — which means that at those peak moments, the thermal stress on the REND1 transformer windings and the associated distribution conductors is substantially elevated above what the real-load requirement alone would impose.

For a food processing and cold storage facility like Foster Farms Livingston, the compressor and refrigeration loads are continuous and non-negotiable. They cannot be curtailed when thermal stress builds. That means the thermal burden accumulates without relief during production windows, and the cooling infrastructure — currently running 106.7 kilowatts of cooling load and burning an estimated $184,879 per year — is working to counteract a problem that originates in the electromagnetic field quality, not in the ambient environment.

The untuned field condition means this stress profile will not self-correct. Without reactive compensation assigned to REND1, the power factor will continue averaging in the low-to-mid eighties, the reactive peak will continue reaching above 1,100 kVAR during high-load events, and the cumulative device stress from repeated sub-nominal voltage dips combined with elevated current will continue aging equipment on an accelerated curve. In an industrial food processing environment, that trajectory leads to unplanned downtime — and unplanned downtime in cold storage and rendering is not an abstract operational inconvenience.

**Priority 1 — Reactive Compensation Assignment.**
The single highest-leverage action for REND1 is MPTS assignment. At 1,113.9 kVAR peak reactive demand and a sustained 641.9 kVAR average, the reactive burden on this transformer is not a marginal inefficiency — it is a structural field problem. Three H490 units sized at 400 kVAR each provide appropriate correction capacity. Engineering should confirm bus configuration, harmonic interaction screening at 5.8 percent iTHD, and physical installation siting for the MPTS cabinets.

**Priority 2 — Sub-Nominal Voltage Dip Investigation.**
Twelve labeled voltage dip events in a single thirty-day period, all clustering in the 455 to 461 volt range, warrant a bus-level investigation. The root cause could involve transformer tap settings, upstream impedance under heavy reactive loading, or distribution conductor sizing. With MPTS correction reducing reactive current, a portion of the voltage dip severity should improve — but tap position and conductor adequacy should be confirmed independently.

**Priority 3 — Peak Current Thermal Profile Review.**
The 1,701.1 amp peak current reading should be cross-referenced against the REND1 transformer nameplate rating and the associated conductor ampacity. At a sustained power factor of 83.4 percent, the transformer is carrying significantly more apparent current than the real load justifies. Engineering should verify that transformer nameplate kVA rating is not being approached or exceeded during peak production windows, and that conductor insulation ratings are appropriate for the observed peak current and thermal environment.

**Priority 4 — Harmonic Interaction Screening Pre-MPTS.**
Before finalizing MPTS unit configuration, a harmonic interaction study should confirm that the existing 5.8 percent iTHD does not create resonance conditions with the capacitive compensation introduced by the H490 units. Standard screening protocol applies; this is a precautionary step, not an indicator of a known problem.

**Priority 5 — Scheduled Downtime Optimization.**
The production pattern shows approximately 25 to 30 percent of the month in shutdown or reduced-load state. Engineering review of transformer de-energization versus standby mode during extended weekend shutdowns may offer incremental no-load loss reduction opportunities in parallel with MPTS correction.

This field is not drifting toward acceptable performance on its own. Untuned reactive fields trend toward higher losses as motor loads age and insulation resistance decreases. That's electromagnetic stewardship — and that's the Unity standard. ---
